definition: Automation in construction is the combination of methods, processes, and systems that allow for greater machine autonomy in construction activities.
details: Construction automation may have multiple goals, including but not limited to, reducing jobsite injuries, decreasing activity completion times, and assisting with quality control and quality assurance. Some systems may be fielded as a direct response to increasing skilled labor shortages in some countries. Opponents claim that increased automation may lead to less construction jobs and that software leaves heavy equipment vulnerable to hackers. Research insights on this subject are today published in several journals such as Automation in Construction by Elsevier.

explainer.lead: Automation in construction gives machines more responsibility for carrying out building and infrastructure work, rather than requiring people to control every action. It can make activities faster, safer, and more consistent, while also raising concerns about employment and the security of connected heavy equipment.

tiers.eli5: It is a bit like using a dishwasher instead of washing every plate by hand: a machine takes over more of the work, but people still choose the job and check the result. On a construction site, this can help finish tasks sooner, keep workers out of danger, and check that work is done well.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply construction automation by combining methods, processes, and machine systems around activities where greater autonomy could improve safety, completion time, or quality assurance. It may also help when skilled operators are scarce. Deployment must account for quality-checking needs, possible workforce effects, and the risk that software-connected heavy equipment could be hacked.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, automation in construction = methods + processes + systems → greater machine autonomy in construction activities. Relevant evaluation goals include fewer jobsite injuries, shorter activity completion times, and support for quality control and quality assurance. Open concerns include possible reductions in construction employment and software-related cybersecurity vulnerabilities in heavy equipment.

explainer.example: On a site facing a shortage of skilled equipment operators, a contractor introduces an automated system for a repetitive heavy-equipment activity. The machine carries out more of the operation itself, with the project aiming to shorten completion time, reduce workers' exposure to injury, and support quality checks; the contractor must also address the equipment's exposure to hacking.

explainer.intuition: Instead of treating automation as a single machine, think of it as redesigning a construction activity so that equipment can perform more of it independently. The methods, work processes, and technical systems must work together to produce that autonomy.
howItWorks: Choose a construction activity and a goal, such as fewer injuries, faster completion, or better quality checks.
Combine suitable methods, work processes, and machine systems around that activity.
Give the equipment greater autonomy so people no longer control every part of the task.
Assess safety, timing, and quality outcomes while considering labor shortages, employment effects, and equipment security.
explainer.whyItMatters: Construction automation links productivity and quality goals with worker safety and responses to skilled-labor shortages. Its value depends on balancing those goals against possible job losses and new cybersecurity risks.
misconceptions: It is not just a particular robot: it includes the methods, processes, and systems surrounding construction activities.
Greater autonomy does not automatically mean fewer jobs overall; job reduction is a concern raised by opponents, not a guaranteed result.
Safety, speed, and quality improvements are goals of automation, not guaranteed outcomes for every system.
